title: Infra GPU Fleet & CI/CD IaC Playbook
author: Asha Patel
summary: Operational playbook for GPU fleet capacity, cloud accounts & networking, Terraform/IaC modules, and CI/CD build pipelines. Includes capacity planning targets, module naming conventions, pipeline examples, and runbook excerpts for common operational tasks.
body:
Overview

This document consolidates infrastructure engineering guidance for operating Redwood's GPU fleet and related infrastructure. It covers capacity planning and sizing, cloud account organization and networking patterns, Terraform/IaC module conventions, CI/CD and build pipeline standards, and the core runbooks used by oncall and platform engineers. The goal is to provide a single, actionable reference for day-to-day operations and for onboarding new infra engineers.

Scope

- GPU fleet and capacity management (hosted inference, dedicated pools)
- Cloud accounts and project/tenant organization (AWS/GCP/Azure patterns)
- Networking patterns for GPU workloads (VPC design, subnets, egress controls)
- Terraform / IaC module design, versioning, and publishing
- CI/CD pipelines for infra modules and runtime images (build, test, promote)
- Runbooks for capacity incidents, upgrades, and rollback

Ownership and Contacts

- Primary owner: Infrastructure Engineering (infra@redwood.com)
- Runtime GPU team lead: Daniel Kim
- CI/CD & IaC owner: Priya Rao
- Oncall rotation: infra-sre-team (see oncall roster)

Service-Level Targets and Capacity Objectives

- Overall GPU fleet utilization target: 60% long-term average (target range 55-70%).
- Spare capacity buffer: 20% of committed GPU capacity reserved for burst and failover.
- Cold-start SLO for model load: 95% of loads complete within 12s for 8k token context on p4d-equivalent hardware.
- Throughput SLO for production dedicated pools: 99.9% requests served under configured throughput threshold.
- Cost target: continuous optimization with monthly unit-cost reports and quarterly cost-reduction initiatives.

Capacity Planning Process (quarterly)

1. Collect usage telemetry (per-pool GPU-hours, instance types, queue latency, eviction rates). Query: cloud tagging + runtime telemetry dashboards.
2. Forecast growth using trailing 90-day growth rate and product roadmaps.
3. Calculate committed capacity needs: forecasted peak * (1 + spare buffer 20%) + warm-up reserve.
4. Validate instance-type fit: choose instance families where model memory and kv-cache fit comfortably (allow 15% memory headroom).
5. Submit budget & procurement requests (finance + cloud-accounts) two quarters ahead for new regions.

- Deliverable: Capacity plan doc and purchase order request template (attach to Q-plan ticket).

Cloud Accounts & Networking Patterns

Account Organization

- Per-environment accounts/projects: prod, staging, dev, sandbox.
- Per-region sub-accounts for high-cost isolation (e.g., prod-us-west-2, prod-eu-west-1).
- Billing tags: service:, team:, env:, pool: (required).

Networking (AWS examples)

- VPCs: one VPC per environment+region. Use segmented subnets: control-plane (private), runtime-gpu (private, high-throughput), management (restricted private).
- Subnets: allocate /20 for runtime-gpu to allow large scale. Separate subnets per AZ.
- Security groups: least-privilege. GPU runtime nodes allow only control-plane ports and egress to model storage & image registries.
- Egress: central egress VPC or NAT gateways per AZ depending on scale. Use VPC endpoints (S3, ECR, KMS) to reduce NAT costs.
- Network performance: ensure enhanced networking (ENA) and latest drivers enabled on GPU instances. Enable jumbo frames when supported by cloud provider for high-throughput model transfer.

Terraform / IaC Modules: Conventions and Patterns

Module Naming and Versioning

- Naming convention: module/<domain>/<purpose>. Example: module/gpu/instance-pool, module/network/vpc, module/iam/service-role.
- Semantic versioning for published modules: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. Bump MAJOR for breaking changes.
- Module registry: internal registry (artifact-store) with a module manifest. Tag module releases with git tag: module-<name>-vX.Y.Z.

Module Design Guidelines

- Keep modules small and composable (max ~300 LOC). Favor composition over large monolith modules.
- Inputs: validate required inputs with explicit type and description. Use defaults only for non-critical envs.
- Outputs: expose only consumable resource IDs and connection endpoints. Avoid leaking raw resource maps.
- State strategy: remote state per environment and per logical unit (e.g., networking state separate from runtime state). Use locking (DynamoDB for AWS).
- Secrets: Never store plaintext secrets in state. Integrate with KMS/HSM or secrets manager for credentials.

Example module variables table (text):

| variable | type | description | required | default |
|----------|------|-------------|----------|---------|
| name     | string | name prefix | yes | n/a |
| instance_type | string | GPU instance family | yes | p4d.24xlarge |
| min_size | number | autoscaling min | yes | 0 |
| max_size | number | autoscaling max | yes | 100 |

Publishing and Promotion Workflow

1. Merge PR with signed-off module changes.
2. CI runs unit tests (terraform validate, tflint), integration plan (terraform plan against sandbox state).
3. Tag release and publish to internal registry.
4. Bump dependent stacks with safe rollout (canary in staging -> staggered rollout to prod pools).

CI/CD and Build Pipelines

Standards

- Pipelines in GitHub Actions/GitLab CI with shared pipeline templates.
- All IaC changes require: terraform fmt, terraform validate, tflint, unit tests (where applicable), and a terraform plan artifact.
- Merge gating: require 2 reviewers and green CI. Auto-apply only from release pipeline with explicit approval for prod.

Pipeline Stages (example)

- lint -> validate -> unit-tests -> plan -> publish-plan-artifact -> promote.
- For runtime images: build image -> static security scan (Trivy) -> integration smoke test -> push to ECR/GCR -> create image manifest.

Example GitHub Actions steps (concise snippet text):

1. uses: actions/checkout@v4
2. setup terraform, verify version lockfile
3. run: terraform fmt -check
4. run: tflint --module
5. run: terraform init -backend-config=...
6. run: terraform plan -var-file=ci.tfvars -out=plan.tfplan
7. upload artifact: plan.tfplan

Testing and Staging Promotion

- All infra changes must be applied to staging (staging account) and validated by smoke tests before prod promotion.
- Promotion path: staging -> canary prod pool (5% traffic) for 24-72 hours -> full prod. Use rollout automation to observe latency and error metrics during canary.

Runbooks and Operational Playbooks

Runbook: High GPU Queue Latency

Symptoms:
- 95th percentile queue latency > 15s for more than 10 minutes
- Autoscaler not increasing capacity despite backlog

Immediate Actions:
1. Verify autoscaler health: kubectl -n runtime get hpa (or cloud autoscaling groups). Check for API errors.
2. Check instance age/launch failures in cloud console (failed boot, insufficient capacity, quota errors).
3. Inspect recent scaling events and throttled API errors (rate limit) in control-plane logs.
4. If autoscaler healthy but provisioning slow: trigger manual scale up (increase ASG desired count or allocate spare dedicated nodes).
5. If queue persists after scale: identify slowmodels via recent traces and temporarily lower concurrency or route traffic to alternative model variant.
6. If provisioning fails due to quota: open emergency quota request with cloud-accounts and reroute lower-priority workloads.

Post-Incident:
- Create incident ticket, capture timelines, note root cause and action items.
- Add findings to regression-triage. Update autoscaler thresholds if necessary.

Runbook: Node Upgrade (GPU driver / kernel)

Pre-checks:
- Confirm upgrade image tested in staging for at least 48 hours.
- Ensure all nodes have current metrics and alerts acknowledged.
- Rollback image available and tested.

Steps:
1. Drain a single AZ node: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data
2. Replace node (terminate) to allow autoscaling group to provision new instance with updated image.
3. Verify node joins cluster and runtime services start (check node logs and container probes).
4. Run a small smoke test workload (10 requests per minute for 30 minutes).
5. Promote rollout to additional AZs with 10% node batches and observe for 2 hours between batches.
6. If failures observed: pause rollout and rollback to previous image (re-provision nodes).

Tooling and Dashboards

- Core dashboards: GPU fleet overview, per-pool latency, per-model throughput, launch-failure heatmap, autoscaler health, and cost per token.
- Alerts: 95th queue latency > 15s for 10m, launch failure rate > 1% over 10m, average GPU utilization > 90% for 30m (notify capacity planning).
- Ownership: dashboards owned by eng-platform; alert runbooks linked from dashboards.

Oncall and Escalation

- Triage path: oncall -> infra-sre -> runtime team -> capacity team -> cloud-accounts (for quota/provisioning issues).
- Escalation contacts in order (work-hours): infra-sre pager, Daniel Kim, Priya Rao. After-hours: follow oncall escalation policy.

Rollout and Change Management

- All production changes require a Change Request (CR) in change-management with expected impact, rollback plan, and test plan.
- Use feature flags and traffic routing for model rollouts. For infra-level changes (networking, instance-type), run a canary in a non-critical pool first.

Appendix: Useful Commands and Snippets

- Terraform plan (example): terraform init -backend-config=env/prod.tfbackend && terraform plan -var-file=env/prod.tfvars -out=prod.plan
- Manual scale: aws autoscaling set-desired-capacity --auto-scaling-group-name gpu-pool-prod --desired-capacity 50
- Check node logs: kubectl -n runtime logs <pod> -c runtime-agent --since=1h
- Diagnose launch failures: aws ec2 describe-instances --filters Name=tag:pool,Values=gpu-pool-prod --query 'Reservations[].Instances[].[InstanceId,State,LaunchTime,PlatformDetails]'
